meta.title: Who really said "The most hopeful people in the world are the young and the drunk. The first because they have little experience of failure, and the second because they have succeeded in drowning theirs"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Aquinas's words: Summa I-II q.40 a.6 asks whether hope abounds in young men and drunkards (after Aristotle); the 'drowning' punchline is modern.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The most hopeful people in the world are the young and the drunk. The first because they have little experience of failure, and the second because they have succeeded in drowning theirs'?
meta.ogDescription: Aquinas did argue, after Aristotle, that the young and the drunk abound in hope. But the witty 'drowning their failures' wording is not in his Summa.

answer.label: Not Thomas Aquinas — a modern paraphrase
answer.sourceLine: The thought is Aquinas’s, and before him Aristotle’s. Summa Theologiae I-II, q. 40, a. 6 asks “Whether hope abounds in young men and drunkards?” and answers that both are hopeful because they do not see their own shortcomings. The quotable wording, with its punchline about “drowning” failure, appears nowhere in that article and has no documented source.

source.heading: What Aquinas actually wrote

docMeta.dd: “Whether hope abounds in young men and drunkards?”
Fathers of the English Dominican Province, Second and Revised Edition, 1920

source.excerpt: On the contrary, The Philosopher says (Ethic. iii, 8) that “drunken men are hopeful”: and (Rhet. ii, 12) that “the young are full of hope.” … Wherefore youths, through inexperience of obstacles and of their own shortcomings, easily count a thing possible; and consequently are of good hope. Two of these causes are also in those who are in drink—viz. heat and high spirits, on account of wine, and heedlessness of dangers and shortcomings. For the same reason all foolish and thoughtless persons attempt everything and are full of hope.
trail: Wikiquote’s Talk:Thomas Aquinas ↗ lists the line under “Unsourced”. It is not on the main Aquinas page.

The source of the idea is Summa Theologiae I-II, q. 40, a. 6 ↗, “Whether hope abounds in young men and drunkards?”. It credits youthful hope to “inexperience of obstacles” and drunken hope to “heedlessness of dangers and shortcomings”, with no “drowning”.

Aquinas draws on Aristotle’s Rhetoric, Book II ↗ (W. Rhys Roberts translation). There the young “are sanguine; nature warms their blood as though with excess of wine; and besides that, they have as yet met with few disappointments.”
The polished modern version keeps circulating as Aquinas’s own words, for example in Catholic Insight (2025) ↗, which gives no citation.
source.excerptNote: The real passage is closer to diagnosis than to joke. Aquinas says the young and the drunk are hopeful because they overlook dangers and their own shortcomings. Nothing in the article says the drunk have “drowned” their failures.

author.name: Thomas Aquinas
author.heading: About Thomas Aquinas
author.bio: Italian Dominican friar and the most influential theologian of the medieval Church, best known for the Summa Theologiae. His treatment of the passions, including hope, builds closely on Aristotle, whom he calls simply “the Philosopher”. That is where the real young-and-drunk passage comes from.

copyAttribution: "The most hopeful people in the world are the young and the drunk..." — popularly attributed to Thomas Aquinas, but a modern paraphrase. The idea comes from Summa Theologiae I-II, q. 40, a. 6, following Aristotle. The "drowning" line is not in his text.

misattribution.heading: How a medieval question became a one-liner
misattribution.intro: The line is a polished modern restatement of a real scholastic article, with a new punchline added. Here is who contributed what.

items.why: He really did ask “Whether hope abounds in young men and drunkards?” and answered yes, in Summa Theologiae I-II, q. 40, a. 6 ↗. But his reasons are inexperience, high spirits and “heedlessness of dangers and shortcomings”. He never says the drunk have drowned their failures.

Aquinas’s article quotes “the Philosopher” for both halves. In the Rhetoric, Book II ↗, the young are sanguine “as though with excess of wine” and have “met with few disappointments”. That is the nearest ancestor of “little experience of failure”.

The quip-shaped version, with “succeeded in drowning theirs”, has no documented origin. Wikiquote keeps it under “Unsourced” on its talk page ↗, and articles such as Catholic Insight’s ↗ repeat it as Aquinas’s own words without a citation.

misattribution.truthLine: Aquinas’s real words are “youths, through inexperience of obstacles and of their own shortcomings, easily count a thing possible”, and those in drink share “heedlessness of dangers and shortcomings”. The source is Summa Theologiae I-II, q. 40, a. 6 ↗. The “drowning” punchline is a later addition.

context.heading: Why the line sticks
lead: Aquinas’s article is one of the more memorable headings in the Summa. In the middle of a sober treatment of hope as a passion, he stops to ask whether youth and drunkenness cause hope. His answer is almost clinical: both groups expect success because they cannot see the obstacles in front of them.

The modern version turns that diagnosis into a joke. The young have not met failure yet, and the drunk have “drowned” theirs. The pun suits a quotation, but it is not medieval. Writers who want Aquinas’s actual point, including the Dominican friars at Dominicana ↗, use it to contrast this reckless hope with the theological virtue of hope.
context.pull: Youths, through inexperience of obstacles and of their own shortcomings, easily count a thing possible.

sourcesVerified.claim: Summa Theologiae I-II q.40 a.6 is titled 'Whether hope abounds in young men and drunkards?', quotes Aristotle ('drunken men are hopeful'; 'the young are full of hope'), attributes youthful hope to 'inexperience of obstacles and of their own shortcomings' and drunken hope to 'heedlessness of dangers and shortcomings'. It contains no 'drowning' line. The translation is the Second and Revised Edition, 1920, by the Fathers of the English Dominican Province.
CCEL hosts the same article, 'Whether hope abounds in young men and drunkards?', citing the Philosopher on drunken men and the young being hopeful.
Wikiquote's Talk:Thomas Aquinas lists 'The most hopeful people in the world are the young and the drunk...' under its Unsourced section.

Aristotle's Rhetoric Book II (W. Rhys Roberts translation) says the young 'are sanguine; nature warms their blood as though with excess of wine; and besides that, they have as yet met with few disappointments.'
Catholic Insight (Carl Sundell, 2025) presents the popular wording ('According to St. Thomas Aquinas, ...little experience of failures... drowning theirs') with no citation.
Dominicana Journal essay 'Young and Drunk' (Br. Pachomius Walker, O.P., 2021) discusses hope abounding in the young and the drunk and contrasts it with theological hope.
